modules.title: 2.1 From Dalton to the Nuclear Atom
modules.html:
The atom is the smallest particle of an element that can take part in a chemical reaction. Our picture of it was built up over two centuries.

Dalton's atomic theory (1808)

  1. All matter is made of tiny indivisible particles called atoms.
  2. Atoms can neither be created nor destroyed.
  3. Atoms of the same element are identical in mass and properties.
  4. Atoms of different elements differ in mass and properties.
  5. Atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios to form compounds.

Modifications. Atoms are not indivisible — they contain electrons, protons and neutrons. Atoms of the same element are not always identical in mass, because of isotopes. Atoms can be created or destroyed in nuclear reactions. Some compounds (e.g. polymers, non-stoichiometric oxides) do not combine in simple ratios.

Key experiments

  • Thomson (1897) — cathode-ray experiments showed the electron and gave the "plum pudding" model: a sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded in it.
  • Rutherford (1911) — alpha particles fired at gold foil mostly passed straight through, a few deflected, and about 1 in 8000 bounced back. Conclusion: the atom is largely empty space with a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus.
  • Bohr (1913) — electrons occupy fixed circular orbits (shells) of definite energy; light is emitted when an electron falls from a higher to a lower level, giving line spectra.
  • Chadwick (1932) — discovered the neutron, explaining the extra nuclear mass.

examples.q: State two ways in which Dalton's theory has been modified.
examples.a: (i) The atom is divisible into protons, neutrons and electrons. (ii) Atoms of the same element may differ in mass because of isotopes.

examples.q: What did the deflection of a few alpha particles in Rutherford's experiment prove?
examples.a: That the positive charge and almost all the mass of the atom are concentrated in a very small, dense nucleus.

modules.title: 2.2 Atomic Number, Mass Number and Isotopes
modules.html:
The atomic number (Z) is the number of protons in the nucleus; it identifies the element and equals the number of electrons in a neutral atom. The mass number (A) is the total number of protons and neutrons (nucleons). Hence

\( \text{number of neutrons} = A - Z \)

An atom is written \( ^{A}_{Z}\mathrm{X} \), e.g. \( ^{23}_{11}\mathrm{Na} \) has 11 protons, 11 electrons and 12 neutrons. For an ion, adjust the electrons: \( \mathrm{Na^+} \) has 10 electrons; \( \mathrm{O^{2-}} \) has 10 electrons.

Isotopes

Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers — same number of protons, different numbers of neutrons. They have identical chemical properties (same electron configuration) but slightly different physical properties (density, rate of diffusion, mass).

  • Hydrogen: protium \(^1_1\mathrm{H}\), deuterium \(^2_1\mathrm{H}\), tritium \(^3_1\mathrm{H}\).
  • Chlorine: \(^{35}\mathrm{Cl}\) (75%) and \(^{37}\mathrm{Cl}\) (25%).
  • Carbon: \(^{12}\mathrm{C}\), \(^{13}\mathrm{C}\), \(^{14}\mathrm{C}\) (radioactive, used in carbon dating).

Relative atomic mass

The relative atomic mass of an element is the weighted average of the masses of its isotopes compared with 1/12 the mass of one atom of carbon-12:

\( A_r = \dfrac{\sum (\text{isotopic mass} \times \% \text{abundance})}{100} \)

For chlorine: \( A_r = \frac{(35\times75)+(37\times25)}{100} = \frac{2625+925}{100} = 35.5 \).

Isotopes are separated by the mass spectrometer, which ionises the sample, accelerates the ions, deflects them in a magnetic field (lighter ions deflect more) and records the abundance of each mass. Uses of isotopes: cobalt-60 in cancer therapy, iodine-131 for the thyroid, carbon-14 in dating, uranium-235 in nuclear reactors, phosphorus-32 as a tracer in agriculture.

examples.q: An element X has isotopes of mass 63 (69%) and 65 (31%). Find its relative atomic mass.
How many protons, neutrons and electrons are in 27Al3+ (Z = 13)?

modules.title: 2.3 Electron Configuration and Quantum Rules
modules.html:
Electrons occupy shells (principal quantum number n = 1, 2, 3 …) which hold a maximum of \(2n^2\) electrons: 2, 8, 18, 32. Each shell is made of sub-shells — s (1 orbital, 2 electrons), p (3 orbitals, 6 electrons), d (5 orbitals, 10 electrons) and f (7 orbitals, 14 electrons). An orbital is the region where an electron is most likely to be found; s orbitals are spherical, p orbitals are dumb-bell shaped.

The three filling rules

  • Aufbau principle — electrons enter the lowest-energy sub-shell first. Order: 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p 5s 4d 5p …
  • Pauli exclusion principle — no two electrons in an atom can have the same set of four quantum numbers; an orbital holds at most two electrons, and they must have opposite spins (↑↓).
  • Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity — electrons occupy the orbitals of a sub-shell singly, with parallel spins, before any pairing begins.

Examples: Na (11) = 1s²2s²2p⁶3s¹; Cl (17) = 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁵; Ca (20) = 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶4s²; Fe (26) = 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d⁶4s².

Anomalies: chromium is 3d⁵4s¹ and copper is 3d¹⁰4s¹ because half-filled and completely filled d sub-shells are extra stable.

The electrons in the outermost shell are the valence electrons; they determine chemical properties. Sodium (3s¹) loses one electron easily; chlorine (3s²3p⁵) needs one more to complete its octet.

examples.q: Write the electron configuration of sulphur (Z = 16) and state its valency.
examples.a: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁴. It needs two more electrons to complete the octet, so its usual valency is 2.

examples.q: Why is the configuration of copper 3d¹⁰4s¹ and not 3d⁹4s²?
examples.a: A completely filled 3d sub-shell is more stable, so one 4s electron is promoted into 3d.

modules.title: 2.4 The Periodic Table and Periodicity
modules.html:
Mendeleev arranged elements in order of increasing atomic mass and left gaps for undiscovered elements. Moseley's X-ray work showed the true ordering property is the atomic number, giving the modern periodic law: the properties of the elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers.

  • Periods (horizontal rows) — the period number equals the number of occupied shells.
  • Groups (vertical columns) — elements in a group have the same number of valence electrons and therefore similar chemical properties. Group 1 alkali metals, Group 2 alkaline earth metals, Group 7 halogens, Group 8/0 noble gases; the block between Groups 2 and 3 holds the transition elements.

Trends across a period (left → right)

  • Nuclear charge increases while electrons enter the same shell, so atomic radius decreases.
  • Ionisation energy and electronegativity increase.
  • Metallic (electropositive) character decreases; non-metallic character increases.
  • Oxides change from basic (Na2O, MgO) through amphoteric (Al2O3) to acidic (P4O10, SO3).

Trends down a group

  • A new shell is added each time, so atomic radius increases.
  • The outer electron is farther from the nucleus and shielded, so ionisation energy and electronegativity decrease.
  • Metallic character and reactivity of metals increase down a group; reactivity of halogens decreases down Group 7.

Ionisation energy is the minimum energy required to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms: \( \mathrm{M(g) \rightarrow M^+(g) + e^-} \). Successive ionisation energies increase, and a large jump reveals the start of a new inner shell, confirming the group of the element.

Ionic radius: a cation is always smaller than its parent atom (it loses a shell and the remaining electrons are pulled in more tightly), while an anion is always larger (added electrons increase repulsion).

Transition elements have partly filled d orbitals and therefore show variable oxidation states, form coloured ions and complexes, and act as catalysts (Fe in the Haber process, V2O5 in the Contact process, Ni in hydrogenation).

examples.q: Why does atomic radius decrease across a period?
examples.a: The nuclear charge increases while the electrons are added to the same shell, so the stronger attraction pulls the electron cloud closer to the nucleus.

examples.q: An element has the configuration 2,8,7. State its group, period and likely ion.
examples.a: Group 7 (7 valence electrons), Period 3 (3 shells); it gains one electron to form X−.

quiz.q: The smallest particle of an element that can take part in a chemical reaction is the
quiz.solution: An atom is the smallest particle involved in chemical change.

quiz.q: Which statement of Dalton's theory is now known to be wrong?
options: Atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios
Atoms of different elements differ in mass
quiz.solution: Atoms are divisible into protons, neutrons and electrons.

quiz.q: The scientist who discovered the electron was
quiz.solution: J. J. Thomson identified the electron from cathode-ray experiments.

quiz.q: Rutherford's gold foil experiment showed that the atom
options: has a small dense positive nucleus
quiz.solution: Most alpha particles passed through, but a few were strongly deflected by the nucleus.

quiz.q: The neutron was discovered by
quiz.solution: James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932.

quiz.q: The relative charge on a neutron is
quiz.solution: Neutrons are electrically neutral.

quiz.q: The mass of an electron is approximately
options: equal to that of a proton
quiz.solution: An electron is about 1836 times lighter than a proton.

quiz.q: The atomic number of an element is the number of
quiz.solution: Z equals the number of protons in the nucleus.

quiz.q: An atom of 40Ca (Z = 20) contains how many neutrons?
quiz.solution: Neutrons = A − Z = 40 − 20 = 20.

quiz.q: How many electrons are in the ion O2− (Z = 8)?
quiz.solution: 8 electrons plus 2 gained = 10.

quiz.q: Isotopes of an element differ in the number of
quiz.solution: Same Z, different A, so the neutron number differs.

quiz.q: Isotopes of an element have identical
quiz.solution: They have the same electron configuration, hence the same chemistry.

quiz.q: Chlorine consists of 35Cl (75%) and 37Cl (25%). Its relative atomic mass is
The isotope used in carbon dating is
quiz.solution: Carbon-14 is radioactive with a half-life of about 5700 years.

quiz.q: Isotopes are separated using a
quiz.solution: The mass spectrometer deflects ions according to their mass-to-charge ratio.

quiz.q: Relative atomic mass is measured relative to
quiz.solution: The carbon-12 scale is the modern standard.

quiz.q: The maximum number of electrons in the shell n = 3 is
A p sub-shell contains a maximum of
quiz.solution: Three p orbitals × 2 electrons = 6.

quiz.q: The rule stating that orbitals of equal energy are singly filled before pairing is
quiz.solution: Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity.

quiz.q: The principle that an orbital cannot hold more than two electrons of opposite spin is
quiz.solution: The Pauli exclusion principle forbids identical sets of quantum numbers.

quiz.q: The electron configuration of sodium (Z = 11) is
quiz.solution: Eleven electrons fill 1s, 2s, 2p then one enters 3s.

quiz.q: Which sub-shell is filled immediately after 3p?
quiz.solution: 4s is lower in energy than 3d, so it fills first.

quiz.q: The configuration of chromium (Z = 24) is
quiz.solution: A half-filled d sub-shell is more stable, so one 4s electron moves to 3d.

quiz.q: An element with configuration 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁵ belongs to
quiz.solution: Seven valence electrons and three shells.

quiz.q: Valence electrons are those in the
quiz.solution: Outer-shell electrons determine bonding.

quiz.q: The modern periodic law states that properties of elements are a periodic function of their
quiz.solution: Moseley established atomic number as the ordering property.

quiz.q: Mendeleev arranged elements according to increasing
quiz.solution: His table was based on atomic mass.

quiz.q: The number of shells occupied by an element equals its
quiz.solution: Period number = number of occupied shells.

quiz.q: Elements in the same group have the same number of
quiz.solution: That is why they behave similarly.

quiz.q: Group 1 elements are called
quiz.solution: Group 1 metals form alkalis with water.

quiz.q: Across a period from left to right, atomic radius
quiz.solution: Increasing nuclear charge pulls the same shell closer.

quiz.q: Down a group, ionisation energy generally
quiz.solution: The outer electron is farther away and shielded, so it is easier to remove.

quiz.q: Electronegativity is highest in
quiz.solution: Fluorine is the most electronegative element.

quiz.q: Ionisation energy is the energy required to remove an electron from a
quiz.solution: It is defined for gaseous atoms: M(g) → M+(g) + e−.

quiz.q: A sodium ion is smaller than a sodium atom because it
quiz.solution: Loss of the 3s electron removes an entire shell and the remaining electrons are pulled closer.

quiz.q: A chloride ion is larger than a chlorine atom because
quiz.solution: Extra electron–electron repulsion expands the electron cloud.

quiz.q: Aluminium oxide is described as
quiz.solution: Al2O3 reacts with both acids and alkalis.

quiz.q: Across Period 3, the oxides change from
quiz.solution: Na2O and MgO are basic; SO3 and P4O10 are acidic.

quiz.q: Transition elements are characterised by partly filled
quiz.solution: Incomplete d sub-shells give variable oxidation states and coloured ions.

quiz.q: Which of these is used as a catalyst in the Haber process?
quiz.solution: Finely divided iron catalyses the synthesis of ammonia.

quiz.q: Noble gases are unreactive because they have
quiz.solution: Their outer shells are full.

quiz.q: The number of orbitals in a d sub-shell is
quiz.solution: Five d orbitals hold ten electrons.

quiz.q: The shape of an s orbital is
quiz.solution: s orbitals are spherically symmetrical.

quiz.q: Which pair are isotopes?
quiz.solution: Same element, different mass numbers.

quiz.q: Nuclide notation 31 15 P shows that phosphorus has
quiz.solution: Neutrons = 31 − 15 = 16.

quiz.q: A large jump between the 2nd and 3rd ionisation energies of an element suggests it is in
quiz.solution: Two electrons are removed easily; the third comes from an inner shell.

quiz.q: Deuterium differs from protium in having one extra
quiz.solution: Deuterium is 2H with one neutron.

quiz.q: The element with configuration 2,8,2 is
quiz.solution: Twelve electrons corresponds to magnesium.

quiz.q: Radioisotope cobalt-60 is widely used in
quiz.solution: Cobalt-60 gamma rays are used in radiotherapy.

quiz.q: Which particle determines the identity of an element?
quiz.solution: The number of protons (atomic number) defines the element.
